I know this goes against everything that a web app should be, but it what it is. So if we have a single threaded web app (legacy) now all of a sudden we have a requirement to support multiple users at the same time. What are our options: Re-architect the app to be multi threaded Find a way to simulate multi threaded behavior Both are great options, but in this scenario option 1 was out, due to the cost involved in re-writing this app to support multi threading. So that leaves us with option 2; how can we at a cloud infra level easily simulate multi threaded behavior. Turns out if we containerize the app (in this case it was easy enough to do) we orchestrate the app such that for each http request is routed to a new container (ie: every new http request should spin up a new container and request send to it) Options For Running ContainersSo when it comes to running a container in Azure our main options are below Here we need to orchestrate containers, ie: at a minimum for every new http request spin a new one), which means we only have two viable options, Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) or Azure Container Apps (ACA). Both are valid options, each with their own pros/cons, with AKS its a lot more complex we will need to : Think of networking Think of vm’s/vm scale sets for nodes Choose ingress controller and set up ingress rules Identity Plus many more, here is the baseline reference for AKS So in short, as flexible as AKS is its not as easy as something like ACA which is a fully managed version of AKS that abstracts all the complexities of Kubernetes. So for this scenario to prove we can simulate multi threaded experience lets go ahead with ACA. Sample Single Threaded ProgramFor this demo below is a simple C# DotNet app that simulates a single threaded behavior, essentially its doing a lock on a static variable which blocks the whole process for 6 seconds. So when we visit the /test endpoint we lock the whole app. 123456789101112131415161718192021222324252627282930313233343536373839404142434445464748public class Program{ private static readonly object LockObject = new(); public static void Main(string[] args) { var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args); // Add services to the container. builder.Services.AddAuthorization(); builder.Services.AddEndpointsApiExplorer(); builder.Services.AddSwaggerGen(); builder.Services.AddApplicationInsightsTelemetry(); var app = builder.Build(); // Configure the HTTP request pipeline. if (app.Environment.IsDevelopment()) { app.UseSwagger(); app.UseSwaggerUI(); } app.UseAuthorization(); app.MapGet("/test", (HttpContext httpContext) => { if (Monitor.TryEnter(LockObject, new TimeSpan(0, 0, 6))) { try { Thread.Sleep(5000); } finally { Monitor.Exit(LockObject); } } return ("Hello From Container: " + System.Environment.MachineName); }); app.Run(); }} Azure Container AppsFor this demo the easiest way to create the Azure Container Apps environment is through Visual Studio, you right click, publish and go through the menus and in the end VS will create a Container Apps Environment and deploy the code as a container to ACA. Once this is all done, we should have a resource group like below Azure Container Apps ScalingNext we go to the container app (the single threaded api we just deployed) and set up a simple http scale rule that will spin up a new container for every 1 http incoming request. In the example below we set min-replicas to 0 and max to 30 this means that when there is no traffic it will scale down to 0 and at peak it will hit 30. TestingNow go to the url of the container app and hit it simultaneously in browser tabs, when I opened it in multiple browser tabs out of 10 tabs about 7 were served by unique containers and based on the test code above I see it being served by different container ids 1234Tab1: Hello From Container: single-threaded-api-app-20220731--ps4yjjp-66f4885b65-w5s6hTab2: Hello From Container: single-threaded-api-app-20220731--ps4yjjp-66f4885b65-gs8qfTab3: Hello From Container: single-threaded-api-app-20220731--ps4yjjp-66f4885b65-x7grletc So its not 100% every single request goes to a brand new container, but very easily and very quickly with out too much complexity we were able to achieve a 70 - 90% of requests being served with new containers, so in essence we found a quick way to simulate a pseudo - multi threaded experience for our legacy single threaded app with out too much effort.

posts.title: Azure Logic Apps Timeout
posts.text: 🎯 TL;DR: Timeout Control Strategies for Azure Logic Apps Logic Apps default timeout behavior doesn’t match production requirements with HTTP triggers timing out at 3.9 minutes and workflow duration defaulting to 90 days. Problem: No granular timeout control per workflow causing long-running processes in production. Solutions: Global Runtime.Backend.FlowRunTimeout setting (minimum 7 days, affects all workflows) or per-workflow timeout branches using parallel “Delay” action with terminate condition for precise timeout control without impacting other workflows. Recently I got pulled into a production incident where a logic app was running for a long time (long time in this scenario was > 10 minutes), but the intention from the dev crew was they wanted this to time out in 60 seconds. These logic apps were a combination of HTTP triggers and Timer based. Logic App Default Time LimitsFirst things to keep in mind are some default limits. If its a HTTP based trigger the default timeout is around 3.9 minutes For most others the default max run duration of a logic app is 90 days and min is 7 days Ways To Change DefaultsWith that, here are a couple of quick ways to make sure your Logic App times out and terminates within the time frame you set. Lets say if we want our Logic App to run no more than 60 seconds at max then: You can change the setting Runtime.Backend.FlowRunTimeout from the default 90 days to 7 days (keep in mind the minimum for this setting is 7 days which is quite large, refer to this issue : https://github.com/Azure/logicapps/issues/782#issuecomment-1609008805) PRO: This will make sure that the Logic App runs for a maximum of 7 days only (which is quite large) CON: However this will apply to all the Logic Apps in the host/tenant, meaning if you had 15 logic apps then all 15 will have the 7 day limit Have a branch with in the Logic App itself to control the timeout (shown in the below diagram) PRO: You have full control of timeout per Logic App, so some can have 30 second time outs while others 60 seconds etc CON: There will be an extra branch/logic in your logic app Time-Out Branch In Logic AppBelow is how a potential timeout out setting in a Logic App could look like. You create a “Delay” branch and set the desired time limit, in the example below its 2 minutes so if the other flow takes longer than two minutes then the delay will finish, logic app will be terminated and a cancelled status will be returned to the user in the below example. Shout out to my colleague John B for this awesome idea. References Main image was taken from the Azure site Thumbnail image was taken from Azure SVG icons

posts.title: Azure DevTest Labs Policies
posts.text: 🎯 TL;DR: DevTest Labs Policy Configuration with Bicep IaC Azure DevTest Labs documentation covers basic lab deployment but lacks policy configuration examples in Bicep. Problem: Missing guidance on linking policies to DevTest Labs using Infrastructure as Code. Solution: Use Microsoft.DevTestLab/labs/policysets resource with ‘default’ name as parent for policy definitions. Implementation includes VM size restrictions, user VM quotas, and premium SSD limits using evaluator types like AllowedValuesPolicy and MaxValuePolicy with proper threshold configurations. Azure DevTest Labs offers a powerful cloud-based development workstation environment and great alternative to a local development workstation/laptop when it comes to software development. This blog post is not so much talking about the benefits of DevTest Lab, but more about how to create policies for DevTest Labs using Bicep. Although there is a good support for deploying DevTest labs with Bicep, there is little to no documentation when it comes to creating policies for DevTest Labs in Bicep. In this blog post, we will focus on creating policies for DevTest Labs using Bicep and how to go about doing this. A Brief Overview of Azure DevTest LabsAzure DevTest Labs is a managed service that enables developers to quickly create, manage, and share development and test environments. It provides a range of features and tools designed to streamline the development process, minimize costs, and improve overall productivity. By leveraging the power of the cloud, developers can easily spin up virtual machines (VMs) pre-configured with the necessary tools, frameworks, and software needed for their projects. Existing Documentation LimitationsWhile the existing documentation covers various aspects of Azure DevTest Labs, it lacks clear guidance on setting up policies with DevTest Labs in Bicep. This blog post aims to address that gap by providing a Bicep script for creating a DevTest Lab and applying policies to it. Shout out to my colleague Illian Y for persisting and not giving up and finding a away around undocumented features and showing me. Existing Documentation For Creating a DevTest LabThe existing documentation for creating a DevTest Lab is pretty good, but when it comes to creating policies for DevTest Lab this is where the documentation falls short. The documentation does not provide a Bicep script for creating policies for DevTest Labs. Vanilla DevTest Lab1234567891011121314151617181920212223resource lab 'Microsoft.DevTestLab/labs@2018-09-15' = { name: 'testLab' location: 'australiacentral' tags: { tagName1: 'test-tag' tagName2: 'test-tag1' } properties: { environmentPermission: 'Contributor' labStorageType: 'Premium' mandatoryArtifactsResourceIdsLinux: [] mandatoryArtifactsResourceIdsWindows: [] premiumDataDisks: 'Disabled' announcement: { enabled: 'Disabled' expired: false } support: { enabled: 'Enabled' markdown: 'Test' } }} Creating Policies for DevTest Labs in BicepThe documentation states all the possible policies that can be created under the fact name in PolicyProperties Below is a list of three of those policies that can be created in Bicep. Allowed VM Sizes Allowed VMs Per User Allowed Premium SSD Per User Linking the policies to the DevTest LabsThis is the important glue that is missing from the documentation, how to link the policies to the DevTest Labs. The way to do this is to create a resource policySetParent and link it to the DevTest Labs. The policySetParent resource is then used as the parent for the policies. 1234resource policySetParent 'Microsoft.DevTestLab/labs/policysets@2018-09-15' existing = { parent: lab name: 'default'} Allowed VM Sizes1234567891011resource allowedVmSizesPolicies 'Microsoft.DevTestLab/labs/policysets/policies@2018-09-15' = { name: 'allowedVmSizesPolicy' location: location parent: policySetParent properties: { evaluatorType: 'AllowedValuesPolicy' factName: 'LabVmSize' status: 'Enabled' threshold: '["Standard_D4_v2","Standard_E4_v2"]' }} Allowed VM’s per user1234567891011resource allowedVmsPerUserPolicies 'Microsoft.DevTestLab/labs/policysets/policies@2018-09-15' = { name: 'allowedVmsPerUserPolicy' location: location parent: policySetParent properties: { evaluatorType: 'MaxValuePolicy' factName: 'UserOwnedLabVmCount' status: 'Enabled' threshold: '4' }} Allowed Premium SSD Per User1234567891011resource allowedPremiumSSDPerUserPolicies 'Microsoft.DevTestLab/labs/policysets/policies@2018-09-15' = { name: 'allowedPremiumSSDPerUserPolicy' location: location parent: policySetParent properties: { evaluatorType: 'MaxValuePolicy' factName: 'UserOwnedLabPremiumVmCount' status: 'Enabled' threshold: '4' }} References Main & thumbnail image was taken from the Azure site

posts.title: Unzipping and Shuffling GBs of Data Using Azure Functions
posts.text: 🎯 TL;DR: Stream-Based Large File Processing in Azure Functions Processing multi-gigabyte zip files in Azure Functions requires streaming approach due to 1.5GB memory limit on Consumption plan. Problem: Large compressed files cannot be loaded entirely into memory for extraction. Solution: Stream-based unzipping using blob triggers with two implementation options: native .NET ZipArchive (slower but dependency-free) vs SharpZipLib (faster with custom buffer sizes). Architecture includes separate blob containers for zipped/unzipped files with Function App triggered by blob storage events for scalable data processing. Consider this situation: you have a zip file stored in an Azure Blob Storage container (or any other location for that matter). This isn’t just any zip file; it’s large, containing gigabytes of data. It could be big data sets for your machine learning projects, log files, media files, or backups. The specific content isn’t the focus - the size is. The task? We need to unzip this massive file(s) and relocate its contents to a different Azure Blob storage container. This task might seem daunting, especially considering the size of the file and the potential number of files that might be housed within it. Why do we need to do this? The use cases are numerous. Handling large data sets, moving data for analysis, making backups more accessible - these are just a few examples. The key here is that we’re looking for a scalable and reliable solution to handle this task efficiently. Azure Data Factory is arguably a better fit for this sort of task, but In this blog post, we will specifically demonstrate how to establish this process using Azure Functions. Specifically we will try to achieve this within the constraints of the Consumption plan tier, where the maximum memory is capped at 1.5GB, with the supporting roles of Azure CLI and PowerShell in our setup. Setting Up Our Azure EnvironmentBefore we dive into scripting and code, we need to set the stage - that means setting up our Azure environment. We’re going to create a storage account with two containers, one for our Zipped files and the other for Unzipped files. To create this setup, we’ll be using the Azure CLI. Why? Because it’s efficient and lets us script out the whole process if we need to do it again in the future. Install Azure CLI: If you haven’t already installed Azure CLI on your local machine, you can get it from here. Login to Azure: Open your terminal and type the following command to login to your Azure account. You’ll be prompted to enter your credentials. 1az login Create a Resource Group: We’ll need a Resource Group to keep our resources organized. We’ll call this rg-function-app-unzip-test and create it in the eastus location (you can ofcourse choose which ever region you like). 1az group create --name rg-function-app-unzip-test --location eastus Create a Storage Account: Next, we’ll create a storage account within our Resource Group. We’ll name it unziptststorageacct. 1az storage account create --name unziptststorageacct --resource-group rg-function-app-unzip-test --location eastus --sku Standard_LRS Create the Blob Containers: Finally, we’ll create our two containers, ‘Zipped’ and ‘Unzipped’ in the unziptststorageacct storage account. 12az storage container create --name zipped --account-name unziptststorageacctaz storage container create --name unzipped --account-name unziptststorageacct Now your Azure environment is ready with the specific resource group and storage account names you provided! We’ve got our storage account unziptststorageacct and two containers ‘Zipped’ and ‘Unzipped’ set up for our operations. The next step is to create our zip file. Concocting Our Data With PowerShellOur next task is to create a large zip file filled with multiple 100MB files, all brimming with random text. In a real world scenario you would already have these large files, but since we are simulating lets use PowerShell to create them. If you already have an existing zip file with large’ish files for testing, you can skip this step and use that file instead. 123456789101112131415161718192021# Set the number of files we want to create$fileCount = 10# The path where you want to create the TestFiles directory$directory = "C:\_Temp\TestFiles"# Create a new directory for our files if it doesn't already existif(-not (Test-Path -Path $directory)){ New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $directory}# Loop through and create our filesfor ($i=1; $i -le $fileCount; $i++){ # Generate a 100MB file filled with random text and save it in our new directory $fileContent = New-Object byte[] 104857600 (New-Object Random).NextBytes($fileContent) [System.IO.File]::WriteAllBytes("$directory\File$i.txt", $fileContent)}# Now that we have all our files, let's zip them upCompress-Archive -Path "$directory\*" -DestinationPath "$directory.zip" This is a simple script that is creating 10 files, each 100MB in size, and then zipping them up into a single file. The resulting zip file should be around the 1GB in size. Incase you are wondering how we end up with a 1GB+ file by compressing 1GB worth of data? we are generating files filled with random bytes. Compression algorithms work by finding and eliminating redundancy in the data. Since random data has no redundancy, it cannot be compressed. In fact, trying to compress random data can even result in output that is slightly larger than the input, due to the overhead of the compression format. We’ll use this file to test our Azure Function. Azure Function To UnzipWe’re going to create a Function that magically springs into action the moment a blob (our zipped file) lands in the ‘Zipped’ container. This function will stream the data, unzip the files, and stores them neatly as individual files in the ‘Unzipped’ container. Before we begin, ensure that you’ve installed the Azure Functions Core Tools locally. You’d also need the Azure Functions Extension for Visual Studio Code. First lets use the CLI to create our consumption plan function app. We’ll call it unzipfunctionapp and use the unziptststorageacct storage account we created earlier. We’ll also specify the runtime as dotnet and the functions version as 4. We are using the consumption plan to demonstrate that this solution can work within the constraints of the consumption plan, where the maximum memory is capped at 1.5GB. 1az functionapp create --resource-group rg-function-app-unzip-test --consumption-plan-location eastus --runtime dotnet --functions-version 4 --name unzipfunctionapp123 --storage-account unziptststorageacct You might need to change the function name in the example about from ‘unzipfunctionapp123’. This could already be taken; this is because, Azure function app name must have Globally unique name.When you create Azure function app, you specify the name which becomes part of URL .azurewebsites.net If the function app name is already taken you will get an error ‘Website with given name unzipfunctionapp already exists.’ when you run the cli command above. Now that we have a consumption plan function infra, lets see the full code that will do the actual task of unzipping and uploadingThere are two code samples and both are quite similar in their basic approach. They both handle the data in a streaming manner, which allows them to deal with large files without consuming a lot of memory. However, there are some differences in the details of how they handle the streaming, which may have implications for their performance and resource usage: The first code sample uses the ZipArchive class from the .NET Framework, which provides a high-level, user-friendly interface for dealing with zip files. The second code sample uses the ZipInputStream class from the SharpZipLib library, which provides a lower-level, more flexible interface. In the first code sample, the ZipArchive automatically takes care of reading from the blob stream and unzipping the data. It provides an Open method for each entry in the zip file, which returns a stream that you can read the unzipped data from. In the second code sample, you manually read from the ZipInputStream and write to the blob stream using the StreamUtils.Copy method. The second code sample manually handles the buffer size with new byte[4096] for copying data from the zip input stream to the blob output stream. In contrast, the first code sample relies on the default buffer size provided by the UploadFromStreamAsync method. Memory wise both are similar (i.e.: they don’t download the entire zip file into memory), but the first script takes around 20 minutes to process a 1GB zip file (with 10 * 100 MB files), whereas the second script takes about 10 minutes for the same 1GB zip file. This mainly comes down to setting the custom buffer size and the optimizations in the SharpZipLib library First script has the benefit of not importing any custom library, but cant not run on an Azure consumption plan, at the time of this writing, consumption plan has a max 10 minute runtime. Second script can potentially run on a consumption plan, but comes at a cost of having to import a 3rd party library. References Thumbnail image was taken from the Azure site Main image generated by DALL-E

posts.title: Extracting GZip & Tar Files Natively in .NET Without External Libraries
posts.text: 🎯 TL;DR: Native .tar.gz Extraction in .NET 7 Without External Dependencies Processing compressed .tar.gz files in Azure Functions traditionally required external libraries like SharpZipLib. Problem: External dependencies increase complexity and security surface area. Solution: .NET 7 introduces native System.Formats.Tar namespace alongside existing System.IO.Compression for GZip, enabling complete .tar.gz extraction without external dependencies. Implementation uses GZipStream for decompression and TarReader for archive extraction with proper entry type filtering and async operations. IntroductionImagine being in a scenario where a file of type .tar.gz lands in your Azure Blob Storage container. This file, when uncompressed, yields a collection of individual files. The trigger event for the arrival of this file is an Azure function, which springs into action, decompressing the contents and transferring them into a different container. In this context, a team may instinctively reach out for a robust library like SharpZipLib. However, what if there is a mandate to accomplish this without external dependencies? This becomes a reality with .NET 7. In .NET 7, native support for Tar files has been introduced, and GZip is catered to via System.IO.Compression. This means we can decompress a .tar.gz file natively in .NET 7, bypassing any need for external libraries. This post will walk you through this process, providing a practical example using .NET 7 to show how this can be achieved. .NET 7: Native TAR SupportAs of .NET 7, the System.Formats.Tar namespace was introduced to deal with TAR files, adding to the toolkit of .NET developers: System.Formats.Tar.TarFile to pack a directory into a TAR file or extract a TAR file to a directory System.Formats.Tar.TarReader to read a TAR file System.Formats.Tar.TarWriter to write a TAR file These new capabilities significantly simplify the process of working with TAR files in .NET. Lets dive in an have a look at a code sample that demonstrates how to extract a .tar.gz file natively in .NET 7. A Simple Example In .NET 7Below is an example demonstrating the extraction of a .tar.gz file natively in .NET 7 in a simple console app to extract the contents of a .tar.gz file to a directory 1234567891011121314151617181920212223242526272829303132333435363738394041424344454647484950515253using System;using System.IO;using System.IO.Compression;using System.Formats.Tar;class Program{ static void Main(string[] args) { string sourceTarGzFilePath = @"C:\_Temp\test.tar.gz"; string targetDirectory = @"C:\_Temp\ExtractedFiles\"; string tarFilePath = Path.ChangeExtension(sourceTarGzFilePath, ".tar"); Directory.CreateDirectory(targetDirectory); // Decompress the .gz file using (FileStream originalFileStream = File.OpenRead(sourceTarGzFilePath)) { using (FileStream decompressedFileStream = File.Create(tarFilePath)) { using (GZipStream decompressionStream = new GZipStream(originalFileStream, CompressionMode.Decompress)) { decompressionStream.CopyTo(decompressedFileStream); } } } // Extract the .tar file using (FileStream tarStream = File.OpenRead(tarFilePath)) { using (TarReader tarReader = new TarReader(tarStream)) { TarEntry entry; while ((entry = tarReader.GetNextEntryAsync().Result) != null) { if (entry.EntryType is TarEntryType.SymbolicLink or TarEntryType.HardLink or TarEntryType.GlobalExtendedAttributes) { continue; } Console.WriteLine($"Extracting {entry.Name}"); entry.ExtractToFileAsync(Path.Combine(targetDirectory, entry.Name), true).Wait(); } } } // Delete the temporary .tar file File.Delete(tarFilePath); Console.WriteLine("Extraction Completed"); }} You can also find this on GitHub Gist. Wrapping UpThe introduction of System.Formats.Tar in .NET 7 marks a significant milestone for developers dealing with .tar.gz files. It provides us with the ability to decompress these file types natively, without relying on external libraries. This functionality is a game-changer as it reduces complexity, minimizes external dependencies, and enhances the versatility of .NET applications. The new namespace System.Formats.Tar, along with the established System.IO.Compression, effectively handle TAR and GZip files. This considerably simplifies the process, making the .NET environment more self-contained and versatile. References Thumbnail image [was taken from the DotNet brand repo]https://github.com/dotnet/brand) Main image generated by [was taken from the DotNet brand repo]https://github.com/dotnet/brand)

posts.title: AGENTS.md vs Copilot Instructions vs Cursor Rules vs CLAUDE.md: Which AI Context File to Use, and When (2026)
posts.text: TL;DR AGENTS.md is the portable format for project instructions. Most major coding agents read it; Gemini CLI needs a setting. Copilot also has its own instructions, rules for matching paths, custom agents and skills. .github/copilot-instructions.md reaches the most Copilot surfaces. Within an AGENTS.md hierarchy, the nearest applicable file specialises its parents. Your explicit chat instructions take priority for the task. Context files change agent behaviour. The research does not show that they reliably improve correctness, speed or cost. Keep one lean source of verified project rules: AGENTS.md when several tools share the repo, or copilot-instructions.md for a Copilot team. Treat it as an operating guide, not a performance switch. In a hurry? Jump to the quick comparison, then come back for precedence, the research and the decision guide. If you use an AI coding agent every day, whether that’s GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code, Codex or Gemini CLI, you’ve felt this particular flavour of tedium: you keep typing the same rules into every prompt. “Use Vitest, not Jest. Don’t touch /legacy. Named exports only. Return { data, error } from every endpoint.” The agent obeys for one session, you close your editor, and tomorrow you type it all again. That isn’t a prompting problem. It’s a missing context layer: the middle tier between what you ask in the moment (the prompt) and the whole system you build around the model (the harness). That layer has a name now. Several names, actually, and that’s exactly the problem: AGENTS.md, copilot-instructions.md, .cursorrules, CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md, Skills, custom agents. They overlap, they compete, and they keep moving. In 2026 alone, Claude Code started reading AGENTS.md, Windsurf became Devin Desktop, and Copilot’s coding agent became the cloud agent. Almost nobody explains how they fit together or which one you should actually use. This post untangles all of it: what each file is, how they interact, what the research says about whether they even work, and, most importantly, which file to reach for, and when. TL;DR diagram: which file should you use?Here’s the whole decision on one page. The rest of the post explains every box in it. For example, Copilot in VS Code and Claude Code can share one AGENTS.md when there’s no CLAUDE.md. A Copilot team can start with .github/copilot-instructions.md. Cursor users alongside Copilot Chat in Visual Studio need both. A deploy or release procedure belongs in a SKILL.md, whichever instructions the repo uses. First, what is an “AI context file”?When an AI coding agent picks up a task, it first has to orient itself: it explores the file tree, opens manifests and config, and reads whatever documentation it can find. But a README is written for humans. It explains what the project does, not how an agent should work on it: which test command to run, which directories it must leave alone, or that /legacy uses synchronous code on purpose and must not be “modernised”. An AI context file fills that gap. It’s a plain text file, usually Markdown, that hands the agent the operating manual it would otherwise have to guess at: exact build and test commands, conventions that differ from the defaults, architectural boundaries, and the files it should never touch. The intended payoff is simple: give the agent verified commands and boundaries up front so it doesn’t have to rediscover or guess them. Sometimes that cuts exploration and corrections. Sometimes the extra instructions trigger more reading, testing and reasoning instead. That tension is exactly what the 2026 research examines, and we’ll get to it. The naming collision nobody warns you aboutBefore comparing files, clear up one thing that trips up almost everyone: two completely different things are both pronounced “agents dot md”. Project context: root AGENTS.mdThis tells agents how to work in the repo or a particular subtree. It’s plain Markdown without frontmatter, and many coding tools read it. Gemini CLI needs a setting. For example: “FastAPI, Python 3.12. Run uv run pytest. Never touch /legacy.” A custom agent: .github/agents/*.agent.mdThis defines a Copilot specialist you select when you need it. It has a YAML profile: GitHub requires a description, and name falls back to the filename. For example, a test-agent might say: “You are a QA engineer. Write to /tests/ only.” You pick these personas from the agents dropdown in VS Code, the agents panel on GitHub.com, or with /agent in Copilot CLI. Same words, two jobs. Even GitHub’s own “How to write a great agents.md” post is about custom agents, not the root AGENTS.md format. Context files at a glanceThe easiest way to compare these files is by what they do and when they load. Instructions for the whole repoAGENTS.md is the portable option. Codex, Cursor, Devin Desktop, Jules, Zed and supported Copilot surfaces read it, as do recent versions of Claude Code when there’s no CLAUDE.md. Use a root file for shared guidance and nested files for local differences. No frontmatter is required. .github/copilot-instructions.md is Copilot’s native option. It supplies instructions across Chat, the CLI, the cloud agent and code review, with a few surface limitations covered below. It’s plain Markdown, always loaded, and has the widest Copilot support. CLAUDE.md is Claude Code’s native option. It supports @ imports and combines the files it discovers. Personal notes belong in CLAUDE.local.md. Copilot’s CLI, cloud agent and GitHub.com code review, plus Cursor and Zed, also read a root CLAUDE.md. GEMINI.md is Gemini CLI’s default. It combines global, workspace and parent instructions, then discovers subdirectory guidance as needed. Copilot’s CLI, cloud agent and GitHub.com code review, plus Zed, also read a root GEMINI.md. Gemini can share AGENTS.md through context.fileName. Rules for selected files.github/instructions/*.instructions.md targets Copilot rules at matching paths. YAML frontmatter supplies an applyTo glob; optional excludeAgent controls whether the cloud agent or code review receives the file. Support varies by Copilot surface. .cursor/rules/*.mdc gives Cursor rules that can load always, by glob, by the agent’s choice or by an explicit mention. Its frontmatter uses description, globs and alwaysApply. Plain .md files in that folder are ignored; .cursorrules is the legacy format. .devin/rules/*.md gives Devin Desktop rules with an activation mode: always, glob, model decision or manual. It still reads .windsurf/rules/ and .windsurfrules as fallbacks, alongside root and nested AGENTS.md files. Specialists and workflows on demand.github/agents/*.agent.md defines a Copilot persona, not project context. Its YAML profile describes a specialist you select for a task. SKILL.md describes a capability or repeatable workflow. Copilot, Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Gemini CLI support skills. The body loads when invoked or relevant, rather than in every session. A skill lives in its own folder and needs name and description in YAML frontmatter. Most useful project guidance is the same whichever tool you use. Build commands, architecture boundaries and test conventions don’t change with the assistant. Keep that material in one source of truth, then add imports, rules or skills only where you need them. The files, one by oneAGENTS.md: the portable standardThis is the one to start with if more than one tool touches your repo. AGENTS.md grew out of a collaboration across the AI tooling ecosystem, including OpenAI Codex, Amp, Google’s Jules, Cursor and Factory. In December 2025, OpenAI contributed it to the Linux Foundation’s new Agentic AI Foundation, alongside Anthropic’s MCP and Block’s goose, and the foundation now stewards it. Over 60,000 open source projects use it. It’s plain Markdown with no required fields: headings, bullets, commands and examples are enough. “Supported by many agents” hides some important small print, so here’s who actually reads it today: The single most useful behaviour is directory scoping. In a monorepo you can put an AGENTS.md in each package so local guidance specialises the root guidance for that subtree; at the time agents.md was written, the main OpenAI repo had 88 of them. Each tool finds and combines nested files a little differently (the precedence section below maps it out), and Codex adds a practical ceiling: it stops adding project files once the combined size reaches project_doc_max_bytes, 32 KiB by default. One more reason to keep the chain lean. .github/copilot-instructions.md: Copilot’s default instructionsThis is GitHub Copilot’s native instructions file for the whole repository, and it reaches further than any other Copilot instruction file: Copilot Chat on GitHub.com and in every supported IDE, Copilot cloud agent (formerly the coding agent), Copilot CLI and Copilot code review all read it. The one exception is code review in Eclipse, which doesn’t support custom instructions at all. AGENTS.md support is narrower, and the support map above shows where the gap bites: as of October 2026, Copilot Chat on GitHub.com and in Visual Studio, JetBrains, Eclipse and Xcode doesn’t read it. If your team lives in Visual Studio or a JetBrains IDE, copilot-instructions.md is still the file that reaches Copilot Chat. Where a surface reads both files, Copilot gets both, so don’t duplicate rules without a reason. If you genuinely need both (say, Cursor users alongside Copilot Chat in Visual Studio), keep the overlap deliberate and the two files consistent, and check GitHub’s support matrix for the surfaces your team actually uses. .github/instructions/*.instructions.md: rules for matching pathsThese files carry YAML frontmatter with an applyTo glob, so a rule only applies to files that match. It’s how you stop frontend conventions leaking into backend code. An optional excludeAgent key ("code-review" or "cloud-agent") hides a file from one of those two. Support is patchier than for the main instructions file (Copilot Chat on GitHub.com and in Eclipse ignores these files, for example), so check the support matrix before relying on them: 123456---applyTo: "src/backend/**/*.py"---* Use SQLAlchemy 2.0 style (`select()`, not the legacy `Query` API).* Every endpoint returns the { data, error } envelope.* Never import anything from src/frontend. Your main instructions file holds the shared context; *.instructions.md with applyTo targets rules at one slice of the tree. .github/agents/*.agent.md: custom personasThese are the personas from the naming collision section: named specialists you pick from the agents dropdown in VS Code chat, the agents panel on GitHub.com, or with /agent (or the --agent flag) in Copilot CLI. A repository profile lives at .github/agents/<name>.agent.md. GitHub’s custom agent reference requires a description and lets name fall back to the filename; VS Code’s own docs treat every field as optional. Custom agents are still in public preview in JetBrains, Eclipse and Xcode. The GitHub analysis covered in the anatomy section below recommends writing an agent’s boundaries as three explicit tiers: always do, ask first, never do. In practice that looks something like this: Always: run the tests before committing; write only to src/ and tests/. Ask first: database schema changes, new dependencies and CI/CD changes. Never: commit secrets or API keys, edit node_modules/, or delete a failing test to make the build pass. The native files: CLAUDE.md, Cursor rules, GEMINI.md and Devin Desktop rulesEach major tool still ships its own native format. The practical notes that matter: CLAUDE.md is Claude Code’s native file. It supports @path imports (up to four hops deep) and a CLAUDE.local.md for personal, uncommitted notes. Claude concatenates every file it finds rather than letting the nearest one override the rest. Cursor reads AGENTS.md (root and nested) and also picks up a root CLAUDE.md. Its own project rules live in .cursor/rules/ as .mdc files; a plain .md file there is ignored. Frontmatter (description, globs, alwaysApply) decides whether a rule always applies, applies to matching files, gets picked by the agent from its description, or waits for an explicit mention. The single root .cursorrules file is legacy. Gemini CLI uses GEMINI.md by default: a global ~/.gemini/GEMINI.md, files in your workspace and its parent directories, and discovery when a tool touches a subdirectory. It concatenates everything it finds. AGENTS.md isn’t a default filename, so to share it, set context.fileName in settings.json to a string or an array such as ["AGENTS.md", "GEMINI.md"]. Devin Desktop (called Windsurf until June 2026) prefers rules in .devin/rules/*.md, falls back to .windsurf/rules/*.md, and still reads a legacy root .windsurfrules. It discovers AGENTS.md files across the workspace automatically: a root file is always loaded, and a subdirectory file applies only to files in that directory. One Claude Code gotcha: since v2.1.277, it reads AGENTS.md on its own, but only when there’s no CLAUDE.md, .claude/CLAUDE.md or CLAUDE.local.md in your working directory or above it. Add one of those files and Claude stops reading AGENTS.md. Start CLAUDE.md with an @AGENTS.md import (Anthropic says this never causes a double read), or change the Project instructions setting to claude-md-and-agents-md. Watch /init too: by default it pulls in Cursor rules and copilot-instructions.md, but not AGENTS.md. Once it writes a CLAUDE.md, that file takes over unless it imports the shared instructions. Because the core content is usually shared, the cleanest approach is one source of truth plus a small bridge only where you need it. For Claude Code, that bridge is a CLAUDE.md that imports the shared file and adds only what’s unique to Claude: 1234@AGENTS.md## Claude Code only* Use plan mode for any change that touches database migrations. SKILL.md: a capability, not contextSKILL.md is a different animal. AGENTS.md tells the agent about your project; a skill tells it how to perform a specific task (deploy, cut a release, run a migration). Agent Skills started at Anthropic and is now an open format, documented at agentskills.io and supported by Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI and others. Skills are directories, not loose files: Copilot looks for project skills in .github/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md, .claude/skills/ and .agents/skills/. Every SKILL.md needs a name and a description in its frontmatter. Skills use progressive disclosure: the agent sees only the name and description up front, loads the body when the skill is invoked or looks relevant, and pulls in supporting files only as needed. Precedence: who wins when files disagreeFor the AGENTS.md format itself, the portable rule is simple: an explicit chat instruction wins for the task, and the nearest applicable AGENTS.md specialises its parents. Here’s what that looks like when you edit one file in a monorepo: That’s the agents.md guidance, not a universal precedence model for every customisation format. Three rules of thumb hold across tools: Files set defaults; the human has the last word. An explicit instruction in chat overrides whatever the files say, for that task. Across formats, there’s no universal order. Copilot CLI does not promise a fixed order for conflicting instructions, and Claude Code may pick between contradictions arbitrarily. Zed reads only the first match from a fixed list, in which .github/copilot-instructions.md comes before AGENTS.md. In a repo with both (and none of the files ahead of them), Zed reads only the Copilot file. Layer, don’t duplicate. Put universal rules at the root and only the differences in nested files. A contradiction between a root file and a nested one is the easiest way to confuse an agent. Anatomy of a great AGENTS.mdIn November 2025, GitHub’s Matt Nigh analysed more than 2,500 agents.md files across public repositories. His post is written for Copilot custom agents rather than the root AGENTS.md format, and it isn’t a controlled benchmark, but its writing advice transfers well. It recommends covering six core areas: Commands: exact, with flags. uv run pytest tests/ -v, not “run the tests”. Testing: how to run the whole suite and a single test, and what (not) to mock. Project structure: map directories to responsibilities, and name the stack with versions. Code style: only the rules that differ from language defaults (the agent already knows PEP 8 and Prettier). Git workflow: branch naming, commit format, merge strategy. Boundaries: what to never touch. “Never commit secrets” was the most common helpful constraint in the analysis. Beyond the six areas, three habits stood out: put commands early, show a real code snippet instead of paragraphs describing your style, and be specific about the stack (React 18 with TypeScript, Vite and Tailwind, rather than “a React project”). Here’s a minimal example you can copy into a project. At about 30 lines including headings, it sits at the top of the range I’d start with: 1234567891011121314151617181920212223242526272829303132# Invoice APIFastAPI on Python 3.12, PostgreSQL 16, SQLAlchemy 2.0, Alembic, Pydantic v2.## Commands* Dev server: `uv run fastapi dev app/main.py` (port 8000)* All tests: `uv run pytest tests/ -v`* One file: `uv run pytest tests/unit/test_invoices.py -v`* Lint and fix: `uv run ruff check --fix .`* Migrations: `uv run alembic upgrade head`## Project structure* `app/api/v1/`: route handlers only; delegate to services* `app/services/`: business logic* `app/repositories/`: data access through SQLAlchemy, no raw SQL## Code style* Type hints on every signature; route handlers are `async`* Pydantic v2 models for every request and response* Every endpoint returns `{ data, error }`## Testing* pytest-asyncio for async tests, Factory Boy for test data* Never mock the database; use the test database## Git* Branches: `feat/<ticket>-<slug>`; commits follow Conventional Commits## Boundaries* Never modify `app/legacy/`; it is synchronous on purpose* Ask before adding a dependency or a migration* Never commit secrets or `.env` files Start at 20 to 30 lines covering only what the agent gets wrong, then grow the file from real mistakes, not hypothetical ones. Cursor’s docs give the same advice: add a rule only when you see the agent make the same mistake repeatedly. What to leave out (this part matters more than you’d think)Every line you add competes for the agent’s attention, so redundancy isn’t free. Include information the agent can’t infer: Exact build, test and lint commands, with flags. Rules that differ from language defaults. Architecture constraints and boundaries. Project gotchas and warnings about files it must not touch. Leave out information it can already recover: Every script in package.json or the Makefile. Conventions the linter enforces, such as PEP 8 or Prettier. Full API documentation; link to it instead. Generic advice such as “write clean code”. Directory tours and project history. The tool vendors agree. Claude Code’s /doctor checkup proposes cutting directory layouts, dependency lists and architecture overviews from CLAUDE.md while keeping pitfalls, rationale and conventions that differ from the defaults. Cursor’s docs tell you not to copy whole style guides into rules or document every possible command. If that sounds like it contradicts the project structure advice above, it doesn’t. A structure section earns its place when it encodes rules (handlers stay thin, data access goes through repositories), not when it narrates the tree. As the next section shows, plain repository overviews didn’t help agents find the right files any faster. But do these files actually work? The 2026 researchHere’s where most explainers stop and simply assert “yes, use them”. The honest answer is more interesting, because two 2026 studies reached conclusions that seem to point in opposite directions. Study A: faster Codex runsLulla et al. ran OpenAI’s Codex CLI with gpt-5.2-codex on 124 merged pull requests from 10 repositories, under two conditions: with the repository’s root AGENTS.md, and with it removed. Median runtime fell 28.64% (98.6s → 70.3s) and median output tokens fell 16.58% (2,925 → 2,440). Both differences were statistically significant. Input tokens told a muddier story: the mean fell but the median rose slightly, and neither change was significant. This was an efficiency study, not a correctness benchmark. The authors put a full evaluation of output quality out of scope, and instead inspected the agent’s output for 50 randomly sampled tasks against the merged human PRs. It also covered one agent and one model, and only small PRs (100 changed lines or fewer, across five files or fewer). Study B: more cost without a reliable success gainGloaguen et al. from ETH Zurich and LogicStar.ai tested four agent and model combinations: Claude Code with Sonnet 4.5, Codex with GPT-5.2 and with GPT-5.1 mini, and Qwen Code with Qwen3-30B-Coder. They used SWE-bench Lite and CTXbench, a benchmark of 138 tasks built from 12 repositories whose developers had committed their own context files. Files generated by an LLM lowered average resolution rates slightly (by 0.5% on SWE-bench Lite and 2% on CTXbench, neither statistically significant) while raising inference cost by 20% and 23% respectively. Files written by developers did better, improving success by 2.4% on average on CTXbench (for every agent except Claude Code), but that gain wasn’t statistically significant either. They still added steps and cost. The agents did follow instructions: when a file mentioned uv, for example, they used it far more often. What didn’t help was the repository overview. Context files didn’t get agents to the files that needed changing any faster. Side by side, the two studies look like this: A note on versions: I’m quoting version 3 of Study B, from September 2026. Earlier versions called the benchmark AGENTbench and reported a 4% gain for files written by developers, so you may see that figure quoted elsewhere. The studies don’t prove that lean files always win. Together they show that context files change agent behaviour, and that the outcome depends on the file, the task, the agent and the metric. Specific instructions get followed; overviews and generated boilerplate mostly add exploration and cost. Study B’s authors land in a similar place: context files are useful for spelling out unusual practices, and any attempt to boost performance with them should be rigorously evaluated. My synthesis is a testable hypothesis: keep commands, constraints and pitfalls the agent cannot infer; cut the narration it can recover from the repository; then check the result in your own workflow. So, do they work?There are two different questions here, and keeping them separate prevents most of the confusion: Can context files change agent behaviour? Yes. Agents generally follow the concrete commands, boundaries, tools and conventions they’re given. Do they reliably make agents more correct, faster or cheaper? Not reliably. Published results are mixed and vary by model, task, file content and what you measure. My practical recommendation is still to start with one lean context file of verified rules the agent cannot infer. That’s a maintainability and risk management call, not a performance claim: it gives the team one portable place for commands and boundaries while keeping the default context small. Use lean instructions when you have real project knowledge worth preserving. Don’t assume they improve every task. Test the outcome. What this means for your Copilot billOn June 1, 2026, GitHub moved every Copilot plan from premium requests to billing based on usage in GitHub AI Credits. One credit is $0.01 USD, and each interaction is charged at the model’s published rates for input, output and cached tokens (plus cache writes, for models that price them). The exception is annual Copilot Pro and Pro+ subscribers who stayed on premium requests: they keep them, at higher multipliers since June 1, until their annual plan ends. Check which billing model your account shows before comparing numbers. That shift is why context files now matter for cost. Under premium requests, you paid per prompt (or per cloud agent session), and the tool calls an agent made on its own were free. Under AI Credits, agent mode and the cloud agent can make several model calls within a single task, and every one is metered. Running a shell command isn’t billed by itself, but the tool definitions, the output fed back to the model and each subsequent call are all tokens. Your default instructions ride along each time: GitHub’s own docs make the link explicit for code review: consumption “generally increases with pull request size and repository custom instructions”. That gives a good context file four possible cost levers: Fewer corrections. Every “no, use Vitest… no, don’t touch legacy…” extends the conversation and triggers more model calls. Less exploration. A concise map may cut repeated context, tool selection and output reasoning. “May” is doing real work there: Study A’s median input tokens didn’t fall, and Study B shows a noisy file can do the opposite. Fewer failed or repeated sessions. Getting it right first time avoids paying twice for the same task, especially in long cloud agent runs. Shorter runs. Time isn’t billed in AI Credits, but compute can be: Copilot code review’s agentic steps consume GitHub Actions minutes, and Copilot cloud agent runs on a GitHub Actions runner by default. As of October 2026, the individual paid plans look like this: Plan Price Monthly AI Credits Base + flex Copilot Pro $10/month 1,500 1,000 + 500 Copilot Pro+ $39/month 7,000 3,900 + 3,100 Copilot Max $100/month 20,000 10,000 + 10,000 The base credits match your subscription price, never change, and are used first. The flex allotment is designed to adapt as AI economics evolve, so it can change. Past your allowance, extra usage is billed in credits at the same rates per token, within whatever budget you set. Copilot Free and Student include an allowance too, and Copilot Business and Enterprise moved on the same date, with 1,900 and 3,900 credits per user per month, pooled across the organisation or enterprise. Where it all fits: the customisation stackContext files are one layer of a bigger picture. Here’s the whole stack in one map: Read it by when each piece loads: instructions are always loaded, rules for selected paths apply when matching files are in play, prompt files, custom agents and skills load on demand, and MCP servers bring in the outside world. Copilot prompt files are available only in IDEs. This post is about the first box; the others deserve posts of their own. So which file should you actually use?Here’s the decision guide. Start with the tools your team actually uses, then add more files only when they have a distinct job. Several tools share the repoStart with AGENTS.md at the root. Most agents read it natively; Gemini CLI needs context.fileName. If the team also uses Copilot Chat in Visual Studio, JetBrains, Eclipse or Xcode, keep a matching .github/copilot-instructions.md. Those surfaces don’t read AGENTS.md as of October 2026, so keep the overlap deliberate and consistent. Everyone uses CopilotUse .github/copilot-instructions.md for the widest support. AGENTS.md is also an option if you only use VS Code, Copilot CLI and the cloud agent. Different parts of the repo need different rulesFor Copilot, use .github/instructions/*.instructions.md with applyTo globs. Cursor’s .mdc globs and Claude Code’s .claude/rules/ do the same job. In a monorepo, nested AGENTS.md files can specialise the root guidance for each package. You need a bridge for one toolFor instructions just for Claude, use a CLAUDE.md that imports @AGENTS.md. Without that import, adding CLAUDE.md stops Claude Code reading the shared file. For Gemini CLI’s default setup, use GEMINI.md, or add your shared AGENTS.md to context.fileName. You need a specialist or a repeatable workflowUse .github/agents/*.agent.md for a named Copilot specialist you select from the agents dropdown or with /agent. Use SKILL.md for a workflow such as deployment or a release. It loads when needed instead of adding the whole procedure to every session. A conservative setup while the evidence is mixedThe research doesn’t prove this setup performs better. I recommend it because it’s simple, portable and easy to audit, and it keeps the default context small while preserving the project rules you know matter: Start with one lean source of truth: AGENTS.md when several tools share the repo, or .github/copilot-instructions.md if everyone is on Copilot. Keep it to 20 to 30 lines of rules the agent cannot infer, and confirm that each tool actually reads it, natively or through a documented bridge. Add rules for particular paths only when you need them: distinct frontend and backend conventions, a /generated folder, and so on. Use *.instructions.md with applyTo, nested AGENTS.md, or Cursor .mdc globs. Add another tool’s file only for a bridge or a unique feature: a CLAUDE.md import, Gemini’s context.fileName, or a copilot-instructions.md for Copilot Chat outside VS Code. Don’t duplicate shared content without a reason. That’s it: one source of truth and targeted overrides where you need them. Then check that it’s earning its place. The file exists to stop specific, recurring mistakes, so watch for them: if you’ve stopped typing a correction, that line is working; if the agent keeps making the mistake, rewrite the line or delete it. Treat every additional paragraph loaded by default as a cost/benefit hypothesis, not as automatically helpful context. Audit what you already have. Claude Code’s /doctor prompt-audit checks your CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.local.md and AGENTS.md files for references to files or commands that don’t exist and for instructions that contradict each other. The Context Health page in the AI Engineering Coach adds a readiness checklist and uses AI to review your instruction files. The honest limitsSame candour as always, because this is where trust is built: Guidance is not enforcement. Tell Copilot “never use any“ and it usually complies, but it can still slip one in. Anthropic’s docs put it plainly: Claude treats these files “as context, not enforced configuration”. Real enforcement needs human review, hooks or CI. Keep it lean. Start at 20 to 30 lines. Anthropic suggests keeping each CLAUDE.md under 200 lines, Cursor suggests keeping each rule under 500, and Codex stops adding project files at 32 KiB combined by default. Redundancy can be a tax. Study B measured 20% to 23% higher inference cost for generated files. That isn’t a fixed penalty for every long file, but every line is a hypothesis about information the agent needs. Validate every command. A stale command in your context file actively misleads the agent. Avoid contradictions between overlapping files (root vs nested, AGENTS.md vs CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md vs copilot-instructions.md). Several tools resolve them unpredictably. Don’t blindly generate the whole file. /init and its equivalents are a fine starting point; then trim hard. In Study B, generated context files didn’t improve success and did raise cost. My takeAfter digging through the vendor docs and both studies, I’ve landed somewhere less exciting than a headline like “AGENTS.md makes agents 28% faster”, and a lot more useful. The file you pick matters less than what you put in it. Choose the format your tools actually read, keep one source of truth, and spend your effort on the 20 or 30 lines an agent genuinely can’t work out for itself: the test command that actually works, the folder it must never touch, the response shape your API promises. That’s the part both studies agree on. Everything else is narration, and when billing is based on usage, narration rides along on every model call. The landscape is also moving fast. Claude Code started reading AGENTS.md this year, Windsurf became Devin Desktop, and Copilot’s coding agent became the cloud agent. So treat your context file like code: version it, review it, delete the lines that stop earning their place, and check which tools read it every few months. This is the context layer: operating knowledge for agents, kept in version control. Keep it lean, keep it accurate, and check whether it improves the work you actually do. Key takeaways Instructions change agent behaviour, but they don’t reliably improve correctness, speed or cost in every setup. AGENTS.md is the portable format, now read natively by most major agents, including recent versions of Claude Code when there’s no CLAUDE.md. Gemini CLI needs one setting. Copilot’s own files still matter. copilot-instructions.md is the main instructions file Copilot Chat reads outside VS Code; rules for matching paths, custom agents and skills layer on top. Within an AGENTS.md hierarchy, the nearest file specialises its parents. Across formats, precedence varies by tool and is sometimes arbitrary, so avoid contradictions. One Codex study found lower runtime and output tokens with an AGENTS.md; a study covering several agents found context files didn’t generally improve success and raised inference cost by more than 20%. Under Copilot’s current billing, every model call in an agent task is metered. Fewer calls, less context and fewer failed sessions can reduce spend. Start with one lean source of truth, add rules for particular paths when needed, and keep extra files for a bridge or a distinct feature. A line that stops a recurring mistake earns its place; a line that doesn’t is just cost. References AGENTS.md: the open format Writing useful agent instructions, GitHub Blog AGENTS.md and coding agent efficiency, Lulla et al. (2026) Evaluating repository context files, Gloaguen et al. (2026) Custom instructions support matrix, GitHub Docs Custom agents configuration, GitHub Docs Copilot billing for individuals, GitHub Docs Custom instructions with AGENTS.md, OpenAI Codex Docs How Claude remembers your project, Claude Code Docs Context with GEMINI.md files, Gemini CLI Docs Rules, Cursor Docs Agent Skills specification Related posts The Four Types of GitHub Copilot Agents Explained AI Engineering Coach: Measure How You Actually Code with AI Image Credits Cover image generated by Copilot

posts.title: GitHub Copilot Agents Part 2: Harnesses, the Agent Host, Cloud Sandboxes and AI Credits Explained
posts.text: TL;DR The four agent types I described in January are no longer the right map for VS Code. Choose a harness, where the session runs and a model, then set the role and permissions. The Copilot harness is now the default. It shares a runtime with other Copilot products and runs through the Agent Host, so a session can outlive its editor window, but not a stopped host. Cloud sandboxes let work continue without your laptop. Under GitHub AI Credit billing, sub-agents consume tokens at their own models’ rates, so context isolation is still useful, but it isn’t free. In a hurry? Jump to the updated decision guide, then come back for the architecture and the money bit. Ten months is a long time in agent landWhen Part 1 went out on 10 January, I split GitHub Copilot agents into Local, Background, Cloud and Sub-agents. It was a useful way to explain the workflows, but it mixed together where an agent ran, how you interacted with it and how it delegated. Since then, VS Code has moved to weekly releases, GitHub has rebuilt Copilot billing, and the old boxes have stopped lining up with the controls in front of us. The better mental model is one Copilot engine with many cockpits, alongside other providers’ harnesses. This post is a November 2026 snapshot, checked against the primary sources on 3 November, covering VS Code 1.144 and GitHub’s 28 October cloud rollout. What happened to the four typesThe biggest change isn’t a rename. The old categories have been pulled apart into choices you can make separately. %%{init: {"htmlLabels": false, "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": false, "nodeSpacing": 15, "rankSpacing": 30, "padding": 10}}}%% flowchart TB accTitle: From four agent types to three separate choices accDescr: January's Local, Background, Cloud and Sub-agent categories mixed several concepts. November separates the harness, execution environment and model, with Copilot as the default harness. JAN["January: four typesLocal, Background,Cloud and Sub-agents"] NOV["November: three choicesHarnessEnvironmentModel"] DEFAULT["Copilot is the defaultLocal remains for migration"] JAN -->|"separate the concepts"| NOV --> DEFAULT classDef historical fill:#f6f8fa,stroke:#8c959f,color:#000,stroke-dasharray:5 5 classDef focus fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000 classDef data fill:#fff4c2,stroke:#b7950b,color:#000 class JAN historical class NOV focus class DEFAULT data The work we used to divide between Local and Background is converging on the Copilot harness. It became the default for new sessions in VS Code 1.143. Local remains available for editor workflows and integrations that haven’t migrated yet. The coding agent became Copilot cloud agent, and research, plans and branch-only work joined the original pull request workflow. The newer cloud experience defaults to a managed sandbox where that environment choice is offered. Sub-agents haven’t disappeared. They’re still isolated workers, but the delegation tool depends on the harness, and their model calls are metered under AI Credit billing. Two things also need correcting rather than presenting as new features. You could already steer the coding agent while it worked in October 2025. And VS Code’s Autopilot arrived in 1.111 in March 2026, not January. I’ve added notes to Part 1 rather than quietly rewriting its history. The new mental model: harness, environment, modelStart a session by separating the agent loop from the machine running its tools and the model answering its requests. %%{init: {"htmlLabels": false, "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": false, "nodeSpacing": 15, "rankSpacing": 30, "padding": 10}}}%% flowchart TB accTitle: The choices that define an agent session accDescr: Choose a harness, an execution environment and a model. Then choose the role and permission settings supported by that harness. Not every combination is available. H["HarnessCopilot, Local,Claude or Codex"] E["Environmentthis computer or containerremote host or cloud"] M["Model accessCopilot, provider credentialsor supported local models"] R["Then: role and permissionswithin that harness"] H --> E --> M --> R classDef focus fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000 classDef output fill:#e6ffed,stroke:#2da44e,color:#000 classDef data fill:#fff4c2,stroke:#b7950b,color:#000 class H focus class E output class M,R data These are separate choices, not a promise that every combination exists. Cloud is an execution target for the Copilot harness, not a fifth harness. Local only lives in the editor’s Chat view. The naming is a trap worth calling out: Local is a harness name, not a synonym for running on your machine. Copilot, Claude and Codex can also run tools on your machine. None of that guarantees local model inference or that your code stays offline. Changing the model doesn’t change the harness either. A Claude model inside a Copilot session still uses Copilot’s agent loop, tools and customisations. Selecting the Claude harness is a different decision. Copilot: the default starting pointThe Copilot harness uses the Copilot SDK and runs through the Agent Host. Use it for day-to-day coding, background work and sessions you want to open in both the editor and the Agents window. In the Session Target control, choose Copilot, then the model and built-in agent. Ask researches without making changes, Agent implements and validates, and Plan researches an approach for review, also available through /plan. Custom agents appear in the same picker. Local: the editor-bound migration optionLocal uses VS Code’s earlier built-in harness in the extension host. Its session belongs to the editor window, so closing that window stops ongoing work. It isn’t available in the Agents window. Keep it when an integration still depends on Local-specific tools or customisations, not because the word sounds more private. Before migrating, check tool availability, MCP configuration and hooks rather than assuming the files mean the same thing in both harnesses. Claude and Codex: different harnesses, not just modelsClaude integrates Anthropic’s Claude Agent SDK. Codex uses OpenAI’s integration, either through its extension or the experimental Agent Host route. They retain their own agent behaviour and provider-specific configuration. Claude support is enabled by default where policy permits it. Codex requires opting into an integration; the Agent Host route has its own authentication requirements, including Pro+ for the Copilot-backed option. There is an important enterprise caveat: the Claude and Codex harnesses are disabled when Copilot enterprise-managed settings apply, including managed permission or sandbox settings. Separate provider credentials don’t bypass that restriction. The harness guide is the source to check when a target is missing from your picker. One Copilot engine, many cockpitsThis is the architectural change that makes the rest less confusing. VS Code’s Copilot harness, the CLI, the Copilot app, cloud sessions and Copilot code review share the Copilot runtime. Claude and Codex remain separate harnesses. %%{init: {"htmlLabels": false, "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": false, "nodeSpacing": 15, "rankSpacing": 30, "padding": 10}}}%% flowchart TB accTitle: Copilot interfaces share a runtime that applications can also use accDescr: VS Code, Copilot CLI, the Copilot app, cloud sessions and code review share the Copilot harness. The SDK exposes that engine to custom applications. CLIENTS["Copilot clientsVS Code, CLI and appcloud sessionsand code review"] RUNTIME["Shared Copilot harnessagent loop, toolsand customisations"] SDK["Copilot SDKembed in your own app"] CLIENTS -->|"share"| RUNTIME RUNTIME -->|"exposed through"| SDK classDef focus fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000 classDef data fill:#fff4c2,stroke:#b7950b,color:#000 classDef output fill:#e6ffed,stroke:#2da44e,color:#000 class CLIENTS output class RUNTIME focus class SDK data The Copilot SDK became generally available on 2 June, with TypeScript, Python, Go, .NET, Rust and Java SDKs. By default, an SDK drives the Copilot CLI in server mode over JSON-RPC. An experimental in-process transport is also available, so a separate CLI process is the default architecture, not the only one. Standard SDK use needs a Copilot subscription, including the Free tier for personal use. Bring your own key is a separate route that can work without a Copilot subscription, with usage billed by that provider. Sharing a runtime makes instructions, skills, custom agents, hooks and plugins more portable. It doesn’t make every surface identical. Tools, model access, permissions, discovery locations and supported customisations still differ. The migration guide is more useful than copying configuration until the errors stop. Prompt files are a particular migration concern: workflows that depend on the Local harness’s prompt files should move reusable procedures into skills for the Copilot harness. Copilot Memory is another shared capability across supported surfaces, but it isn’t a promise that all personal settings or session history automatically synchronise. One SDK default deserves attention before embedding it in a tool: it exposes the CLI’s first-party tools by default, similar to --allow-all. Execution is still governed by the SDK’s permission handler. Configure that handler and the available tools deliberately rather than treating an embedded agent as a harmless text-completion API. The Agent Host: sessions that outlive the windowThe Agent Host is a dedicated process that owns sessions, their terminals and their changes. The editor window is a client of that process, not the place the whole agent has to live. %%{init: {"htmlLabels": false, "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": false, "nodeSpacing": 15, "rankSpacing": 30, "padding": 10}}}%% flowchart TB accTitle: Clients connect to an Agent Host running beside the code accDescr: The editor, Agents window and browser connect to an Agent Host. The host owns session state and runs harnesses beside the workspace. CLIENT["Editor, Agents windowor browser"] HOST["Agent Hostsession stateterminals and changes"] HARN["Harness adaptersCopilot, Claude and Codex"] CODE["Code and toolsthis computer, a containeror a remote host"] CLIENT -->|"Agent Host Protocol"| HOST HOST --> HARN --> CODE classDef focus fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000 classDef output fill:#e6ffed,stroke:#2da44e,color:#000 class HOST,HARN focus class CLIENT,CODE output Clients communicate through the open Agent Host Protocol. Version 1.0 arrived with VS Code 1.144. The host owns the authoritative state, so several clients can observe and steer the same session instead of each creating a copy. The distinction that matters in practice is session lifetime. Close a project or editor window, and a Copilot harness session can keep working while its Agent Host remains running. Quit the VS Code application that manages that local host, and the work stops. Put the laptop to sleep, and local work doesn’t magically continue elsewhere. A remote session can continue if its remote machine and serving process stay running. A cloud sandbox doesn’t depend on your laptop, although the service still manages its availability and lifecycle. Being able to reopen a conversation isn’t proof that its agent kept working while its host was stopped. For an overnight job, choose a host that will actually stay available. Window independence is not machine independence. Connected windows can lend tools to a session, including extension and browser capabilities. Those tools need their lender to stay connected, even if the host itself can keep going. For a standalone host, the documented command is code agent host; --tunnel exposes it through a dev tunnel. GitHub Environments, currently in preview, lets you register an existing machine and access supported sessions from other Copilot clients. Registration doesn’t provision compute or move your workspace. Your machine still has to stay on. Handoffs have changedPart 1 described a smooth Local to Background to Cloud escalation path. That isn’t a general pipeline inside the current VS Code experience. %%{init: {"htmlLabels": false, "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": false, "nodeSpacing": 15, "rankSpacing": 30, "padding": 10}}}%% flowchart TB accTitle: A VS Code Local session can hand off, but not through an unlimited chain accDescr: A Local session can carry its history to Copilot, Claude or experimental Codex. Those sessions cannot hand off again to another harness or the cloud. LOCAL["VS Code Local session"] DEST["Copilot, Claude orexperimental Codex"] STOP["No further handoffstart a cloud sessionwhen you need the cloud"] LOCAL -->|"history and context"| DEST --> STOP classDef focus fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000 classDef data fill:#fff4c2,stroke:#b7950b,color:#000 classDef warning fill:#ffd6d6,stroke:#c0392b,color:#000 class LOCAL data class DEST focus class STOP warning A Local session can hand off to Copilot, Claude or the experimental Codex integration, carrying its conversation history and context. Those destination sessions can’t then hand off to another harness or to the cloud. Starting a new cloud session is a separate operation; it doesn’t automatically copy your local uncommitted changes. The terminal CLI still supports /delegate, or a prompt beginning with &. That delegates a task to Copilot cloud agent, creating a branch and draft PR. It isn’t the same operation as selecting another harness in VS Code. For an interactive CLI session whose tools run in a cloud sandbox, start it with: 1copilot --cloud That starts a new cloud session rather than moving the current local conversation. Once a cloud sandbox session exists, supported clients can reconnect to the same session. Continuing a session, handing off a task and starting another session are three different things. The cloud side: Copilot cloud agent and cloud sandboxesThe cloud agent has grown beyond “assign an issue and wait for a PR”. You can ask for research, approve a plan before implementation, iterate on a branch and request a PR when you’re ready. The newer connected experience also changes where that work runs. Check the selected environment before starting, because the default and available choices still depend on the client and workflow. %%{init: {"htmlLabels": false, "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": false, "nodeSpacing": 15, "rankSpacing": 30, "padding": 10}}}%% flowchart TB accTitle: Choose Actions when the repository needs Actions-specific capabilities accDescr: Use Actions for Actions setup steps, runner customisation or Windows. Otherwise, a managed Linux cloud sandbox is the default where offered. START["Need Actions-specificsetup, runners or Windows?"] ACTIONS["Actions"] CLOUD["Cloud sandbox"] START -->|"yes"| ACTIONS START -->|"no"| CLOUD classDef focus fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000 classDef output fill:#e6ffed,stroke:#2da44e,color:#000 classDef data fill:#fff4c2,stroke:#b7950b,color:#000 class START focus class CLOUD output class ACTIONS data Cloud sandboxes: the new default where offeredA cloud sandbox is a GitHub-hosted Linux environment with its own workspace. It can keep working without your machine, saves a snapshot when stopped and can resume across supported Copilot clients. Unlike Actions-based agent sessions, sandboxes don’t have the one-hour total running-time limit. They can also work across repositories in one organisation, or across repositories owned by your personal account. Access and organisation policies still apply. The connected cloud experience and sandboxes became generally available on paid Copilot plans on 28 October. Entry points include GitHub.com, Mobile, the CLI, the Copilot app, VS Code, Slack and Teams. Availability in a service doesn’t mean every client’s integration has the same maturity. Actions: still needed for some repositoriesChoose Actions when the repository needs copilot-setup-steps.yml, Actions-specific setup such as OIDC sign-in, larger or self-hosted runners, or a Windows environment. Those settings don’t automatically transfer into a cloud sandbox. Actions-based agent sessions still have a 59-minute execution limit and are scoped to one repository. GitHub also documents a one-branch, one-pull-request-per-task limitation. A sandbox’s broader repository access isn’t a promise of unlimited PR creation within one task. Remote environments: your compute, your lifecycleA registered machine or VM is another option when you need an environment you control. Unlike a managed sandbox, you maintain the machine, dependencies and uptime. Automations can initiate recurring work on schedules or repository events, subject to feature availability, eligible repositories and policy. A cloud automation doesn’t need your laptop; an automation running locally still needs its host. Security checks are defaults, not an absolute guaranteePart 1 called security validation non-negotiable. The current security documentation says repository administrators can disable individual validation tools. By default, the cloud agent uses CodeQL, secret scanning and checks of new dependencies against the GitHub Advisory Database. The validation doesn’t require a GitHub Advanced Security licence. Keep it enabled, inspect the results and review the code yourself. Automated scanning isn’t proof that a change is safe. Claude and Codex are also available as third-party coding agents on GitHub, currently in public preview and subject to account policies. They receive security validation and consume AI credits plus Actions minutes. Don’t confuse those hosted agents with simply selecting one of their models inside Copilot. Sub-agents: the same context benefit, a different billThe useful part of Part 1 still stands. A worker can investigate a bounded question in its own context and return a focused answer, without filling the main thread with every file read and intermediate result. %%{init: {"htmlLabels": false, "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": false, "nodeSpacing": 15, "rankSpacing": 30, "padding": 10}}}%% flowchart TB accTitle: Isolated workers return focused results to the main agent accDescr: The main agent delegates independent research and review tasks to workers with their own context. Focused results return to the main agent for implementation. Each worker's model calls contribute to usage. MAIN["Main agentassigns scoped tasks"] RESEARCH["Researcherown context"] REVIEW["Reviewerown context"] RESULTS["Focused resultsnot every intermediate step"] NEXT["Main agentimplements and validates"] MAIN --> RESEARCH & REVIEW RESEARCH & REVIEW --> RESULTS --> NEXT classDef focus fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000 classDef data fill:#fff4c2,stroke:#b7950b,color:#000 classDef output fill:#e6ffed,stroke:#2da44e,color:#000 class MAIN,NEXT focus class RESEARCH,REVIEW data class RESULTS output The delegation mechanism now depends on the harness. Copilot uses its native task tool; Local uses runSubagent, exposed through the agent tool set. Claude and Codex manage their own provider-native sub-agents. That is more than a spelling change. When migrating a coordinator, review its tool list, prompts and expected arguments. Don’t mechanically replace runSubagent with task and assume the contracts match. Give a research worker a smaller job and modelFor a Local harness example, create .github/agents/repo-researcher.agent.md with a read-only tool list and a model suited to lightweight research: 12345678910111213141516---name: Repo Researcherdescription: >- Find files and patterns.
