Never edit.user-invocable: falsetools: ['read', 'search']model: >- Claude Haiku 4.5 (copilot)---Research the assigned topic.Do not change any files.Return the relevant paths,the existing pattern andany unanswered questions.Use fewer than 200 words. This is a Local harness example, not a universal configuration for all four harnesses. Choose an available model from your picker and compare its current price with the parent model. user-invocable: false hides the worker from the picker without preventing agent invocation. Local’s model selection order is an explicit tool-call preference, then the custom agent’s model, then Auto if chat.subagents.defaultToAuto is enabled and applicable, then the parent model. Explicit and agent-configured selections can’t exceed the parent’s cost tier. Auto routing has separate rules, so that isn’t a universal guarantee that a worker can never use a pricier model. Local invocations are stateless and don’t inherit the conversation history. Supply the goal, necessary context, allowed actions and expected result. Nested Local sub-agents are off by default; enabling chat.subagents.allowInvocationsFromSubagents permits nesting up to five levels. Make the cost visibleEnable chat.subagents.showCreditUsage to show credit usage in the worker’s response pill and hover details. It is hidden by default. In the Agents window, you can inspect a worker’s model, elapsed time and active tool call. Delegation adds model usage and coordination. Use it when separate context, independent work or a cheaper model is worth that overhead. A quick lookup doesn’t need a miniature organisation of agents. Guardrails: permissions, Autopilot and sandboxingThere are three separate controls here, and confusing them is an easy way to grant more autonomy than you meant to. %%{init: {"htmlLabels": false, "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": false, "nodeSpacing": 15, "rankSpacing": 30, "padding": 10}}}%% flowchart TB accTitle: Permissions, Autopilot and terminal sandboxing are separate controls accDescr: Permission levels govern approvals. The workflow mode controls how autonomously the agent continues. Terminal sandboxing is a separate layer and does not cover every tool. PERM["ApprovalsManual, Assistedor Allow all"] AUTO["WorkflowAgent or Autopilot"] SBX["Terminal sandboxfile and network limits"] LIMIT["Other tools needtheir own controls"] PERM -->|"combine with"| AUTO AUTO -->|"separate layer"| SBX SBX --- LIMIT classDef focus fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000 classDef data fill:#fff4c2,stroke:#b7950b,color:#000 classDef warning fill:#ffd6d6,stroke:#c0392b,color:#000 class PERM focus class AUTO,SBX data class LIMIT warning In Copilot harness sessions, Manual permissions follows your configured approval rules. Assisted uses an LLM judge to assess tool calls and asks you about those it doesn’t approve. Allow all runs tools without confirmation. Assisted became generally available in VS Code 1.144 and requires Folder isolation. Worktree sessions always use Allow all. A worktree separates Git changes; it doesn’t isolate the agent from the rest of your machine. Autopilot is an agent mode in the Copilot harness, not another permission level. It auto-approves tools, retries errors and answers questions that would otherwise block progress. In the Local harness, Autopilot is still selected as a permission level. That harness-specific difference matters when following older instructions. Sandboxing is separate again. An enabled terminal sandbox restricts file system and network access even under Allow all or Autopilot. It doesn’t cover every tool, so it isn’t a substitute for tool and URL controls. Local terminal sandboxing is in preview on macOS, Linux and WSL2, and experimental on Windows. Neither Assisted nor Autopilot guarantees good judgement. Both can make mistakes, and their model usage belongs in your cost planning too. The money bit: from premium requests to AI creditsGitHub moved Copilot to usage-based billing on 1 June 2026. One GitHub AI Credit is $0.01 USD, and metered model usage is priced from input, output and cached tokens at the selected model’s rates. The important unit is no longer just the prompt you typed. An agent task can make many model calls, with more calls in its workers. %%{init: {"htmlLabels": false, "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": false, "nodeSpacing": 15, "rankSpacing": 30, "padding": 10}}}%% flowchart TB accTitle: Every model call in an agent task contributes to usage accDescr: Main-agent and worker model calls consume input, output and cached tokens at each model's rates. These costs draw from the AI Credit allowance and permitted additional usage. PROMPT["One user task"] CALLS["Main and workermodel calls"] TOKENS["Input, outputand cached tokensat each model's rates"] AI["GitHub AI Creditsincluded allowance,then permitted extra usage"] PROMPT --> CALLS --> TOKENS --> AI classDef focus fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#000 classDef warning fill:#ffd6d6,stroke:#c0392b,color:#000 class PROMPT,CALLS focus class TOKENS,AI warning Under legacy premium-request billing, user prompts or cloud agent sessions were the relevant units, with model multipliers. Tool calls made within an agent’s work weren’t each a new user request. That’s the context behind Part 1’s advice about effectively free sub-agents. Under AI Credit billing, worker model calls consume usage at their own models’ rates. A shell command isn’t itself a model call, but its output can become input to the next one. Repeated context and long conversations still count, although cached input may have a different price. Check the billing model before comparing numbersSome existing annual Pro and Pro+ subscribers chose to remain on legacy premium-request billing until their annual plan ends. Those accounts are an exception to the general migration, not evidence that worker model calls are free on usage-based plans. Inline code completions and next edit suggestions aren’t billed in AI credits. Nor are responses actually run by the experimental on-device model. A local harness calling a hosted model is not that on-device exception. Copilot Fusion also isn’t free routing. It bills the models it uses at their standard rates, with the current 30% paid-plan discount running through 30 November 2026. Treat model usage and cloud execution as separate budgetsCloud sandboxes have compute, allocated-memory and stopped-snapshot-storage meters. Compute and memory can draw from the shared included compute entitlement also used by eligible Actions runners. That isn’t your AI Credit allowance. GitHub announced sandbox billing would begin in November 2026. Check the sandbox billing documentation for the applicable rates and controls. Stopping a sandbox stops compute and memory metering, but retained snapshots still consume storage. An AI Credit budget alone doesn’t cap sandbox spending. Configure the relevant product or SKU budget too, and enable its stop-usage option when you need a hard limit rather than an alert. What I’d do about itGive workers cheaper models when the task allows it, keep their briefs bounded and avoid sending the same large context to several agents without a reason. Keep the main thread focused rather than paying a frontier model to repeatedly reread everything. For teams, included usage is pooled: Business contributes 1,900 AI credits per seat per month and Enterprise contributes 3,900. User-level budgets cap total consumption, including usage drawn from the pool; spending limits at other levels can control additional charges. Those are different controls, so check which one you’re setting. The point isn’t to avoid delegation. It’s to stop treating delegation, Fusion and Autopilot as invisible work outside the meter. Part 1’s decision guide, rewrittenPair on code or plan a changeStart with the Copilot harness in the Chat view. Use Ask to understand the code, Plan to review an approach and Agent to implement it. Choose a different harness for its behaviour or integrations, not simply because you want one of its provider’s models. Keep working after closing an editor windowUse an Agent Host-backed Copilot session and keep VS Code and the host running. If the requirement is “keep working with my laptop shut”, choose a remote machine that stays on or a cloud sandbox instead. Fix an issue overnight and review it in the morningUse a cloud session with clear acceptance criteria. Ask for a plan first when the approach needs review, or ask explicitly for a pull request. Select Actions if the repository depends on Actions-specific setup or runners. Work on several features without mixing the changesUse separate sessions and worktrees in the Agents window. This isolates Git changes, not security permissions. Compare the extra model usage with the value of independent work. Research without filling the main contextUse a bounded sub-agent on an appropriate cheaper model. Give it enough context to work independently and ask for a concise result. For a small lookup, stay in the main session. Reuse a provider workflow, schedule a job or embed an agentChoose Claude or Codex when you need their native harness and policy permits it. Use an automation for a recurring job, selecting a host that will be available when it runs. Use the Copilot SDK to put the Copilot runtime inside your own application. Keep Local only for a workflow that still needs it while you migrate. How we got hereThe release dates make the pace easier to appreciate: 25 February: the Copilot CLI became generally available. 9 March: VS Code 1.111 began weekly Stable releases and introduced Autopilot. 1 April: the renamed cloud agent added branch-only work and plans. 1 and 2 June: AI Credit billing went live, followed by Copilot SDK general availability. 17 June: the Copilot app became generally available. 15 July: VS Code 1.129 began rolling out the Agent Host. October: 1.143 made the Copilot harness the default; 28 October brought the connected cloud experience and VS Code 1.144 with AHP 1.0. Those changes explain why a January comparison table now needs more than a few renamed columns. Honest limitsCloud sandboxes are generally available, but VS Code’s cloud-session integration still has experimental settings and account requirements. The Dev Container and direct Codex integrations also have their own maturity and setup constraints. The Copilot harness doesn’t yet expose every Local tool or customisation. Enterprise policy can restrict harnesses, models, permissions and environments, or move a Local session to Copilot so the runtime can enforce the policy. The docs describe several overlapping generations of workflows. When checking sub-agents and permissions, use the documentation for your actual harness. When checking cloud behaviour, distinguish managed sandboxes from Actions-based sessions. This will date again. Treat the dates, preview labels and discounts as a snapshot, not permanent promises. My takeThe headline isn’t any single feature. It’s convergence. In January I was explaining four agents with four rulebooks. Today the useful questions are which harness should run the loop, where its tools should run and which model should do the thinking. For Copilot, one engine with many cockpits is a much better mental model. Just don’t mistake a common engine for identical capabilities everywhere, or a persistent conversation for compute that never stops. The bit I’d flag to every team lead is cost. Sub-agents remain a useful context-management tool, but every worker needs to earn its model usage. Give it a bounded job, choose its model deliberately and turn the credit meter on. Key takeaways Choose the harness, execution environment and model separately. Local is a harness name, not a privacy or offline guarantee. Agent Host sessions can outlive an editor window, but they still need a running host. Use remote or cloud compute for work that must outlive your laptop. Cloud sandboxes bring resumable sessions and broader repository scope; Actions remains necessary for some setup and runner requirements. Delegation tools and permission semantics depend on the harness. Review integrations rather than relying on old tool names. Under AI Credit billing, the main agent and its workers all contribute model usage. Cloud execution has separate meters and budget controls. References Choose an agent harness, VS Code Agent Host architecture, VS Code Use subagents, VS Code Manage approvals and permissions, VS Code VS Code 1.144 release notes GitHub Copilot SDK: architecture, authentication and tools Copilot on GitHub.com and GitHub Mobile: environments and limitations Cloud sandboxes: defaults, setup compatibility and lifecycle Billing for cloud and local sandboxes AI Credit billing for individuals AI Credit billing for organisations and enterprises Legacy billing exceptions for existing annual plans Related posts Part 1: The Four Types of GitHub Copilot Agents, preserved with update notes as a historical snapshot. AGENTS.md vs Copilot Instructions vs Cursor Rules vs CLAUDE.md, for the context files and customisations around the agent. Image Credits Cover image generated by Copilot

pages.title: Cookie Policy & Privacy Information
pages.text: Your privacy is respected. This blog is a static website hosted on GitHub Pages. No backend databases are operated, and no personal information is stored on the servers. All content is publicly available on GitHub. The only data collection that occurs is through third-party services (detailed below) that help understand site usage and provide enhanced functionality. To learn more about how this blog is built, see the Hello World 👋 blog post which details all the technology and hosting infrastructure used, including GitHub Pages. This website uses cookies to enhance browsing experience and provide certain functionality. By using this site, consent to the use of cookies in accordance with this policy is given. What Are Cookies?Cookies are small text files that are placed on your computer or mobile device when you visit a website. They are widely used to make websites work more efficiently and provide information to website owners. Learn more about cookies on Wikipedia. Cookies UsedEssential CookiesThese cookies are necessary for the website to function properly: Session cookies: Maintain sessions while browsing Analytics CookiesGoogle Analytics is used to understand how visitors interact with the website: Google Analytics Purpose: Analyze site traffic, page views, and user behavior Data collected: Pages visited, time spent, browser type, device type, geographic location Retention: Up to 26 months Google Analytics Privacy Policy Advertising CookiesAdvertisements are displayed through Google AdSense: Google AdSense Purpose: Display relevant advertisements Data collected: Browsing behavior, interests, demographic information Google Ads Privacy Policy Social Sharing CookiesShareThis is used for social media sharing: ShareThis Purpose: Enable content sharing on social media platforms Data collected: Pages shared, social media interactions ShareThis Privacy Policy Comment System CookiesDisqus is used for comments: Disqus Purpose: Provide commenting functionality Data collected: Username, email, comment content, IP address Disqus Privacy Policy Managing CookiesBrowser SettingsYou can control and/or delete cookies as you wish. You can delete all cookies that are already on your computer and you can set most browsers to prevent them from being placed. Chrome: Settings → Privacy and security → Cookies and other site data Firefox: Settings → Privacy & Security → Cookies and Site Data Safari: Preferences → Privacy → Cookies and website data Edge: Settings → Cookies and site permissions Opt-Out Options Google Analytics: Install the Google Analytics Opt-out Browser Add-on Google Ads: Visit Google Ads Settings Do Not Track: Enable “Do Not Track” in your browser settings Declining CookiesWhen you first visit this site, you’ll see a cookie consent banner. You can choose to: Allow cookies: Accept all cookies for full functionality Decline: Reject non-essential cookies (may limit some features) Third-Party LinksThis website may contain links to third-party websites. No responsibility is taken for the privacy practices or content of those websites. Their privacy policies should be reviewed separately. Data Retention Google Analytics: Data is retained for 26 months AdSense: Data retention varies based on Google’s policies Disqus: Comment data is retained indefinitely unless deleted by the user Contact InformationQuestions about this cookie policy can be directed to: GitHub: github.com/Ricky-G LinkedIn: linkedin.com/in/rickygummadi Changes to This PolicyThis cookie policy may be updated from time to time. Any changes will be posted on this page with an updated revision date. Last Updated: December 29, 2025 Additional Resources About Cookies EU Cookie Law GDPR Information

pages.title: Hi 👋, I'm Ricky
pages.text: Thanks for stopping by 🙂!! I am Ricky Gummadi, based in Auckland, New Zealand. I write about building intelligent applications on Azure, from AI agents and LLMs to cloud-native architecture and everything in between. As Scott Hanselman said “if you get asked a good question, you should post it to share rather than reply by email” and this is the medium for me to do just that. During the day I work for Microsoft as a Cloud & AI architect, where I help organisations architect AI-powered solutions on Azure. In the evenings I work on my own projects and private consulting. Please note that all opinions, insights, and content shared on this blog are my personal views and do not represent the official position or policies of Microsoft or any other organization I may be affiliated with. 👍🏻 Feel free to connect with me on LinkedIn Connect on LinkedIn How This Blog Was BuiltBefore AI coding assistants were a thing, I set out to build this blog the old-fashioned way evaluating frameworks, weighing trade-offs, and making deliberate choices. Here is the short version (the full story is in my Hello World 👋 post). Requirements were simple: easy to author (Markdown), easy to build, easy to maintain, and most features (search, tags, categories) should work out of the box. Hosting had to be free, handle reasonable traffic, and support CI/CD. I evaluated: Orchard CMS, Hugo, Ghost, Jekyll + GitHub Pages, and Hexo. Hugo was impressive but geared more towards generic sites. Jekyll + GitHub Pages was strong but meant learning Ruby tooling. Hexo a dedicated JavaScript-based static site generator checked every box and came with 360+ community themes. The stack I landed on: Hexo Generates the entire blog as a static site from Markdown files Icarus theme Clean, feature-rich, and community maintained GitHub Pages Free hosting with a 100 GB bandwidth soft limit GitHub Actions Builds and deploys the site automatically on every push Bulma CSS framework to enrich styling beyond plain Markdown The result is a zero-cost, low-maintenance blog where I write in Markdown, push to GitHub, and the site is live within minutes. No databases, no servers, no ongoing costs. Tech Stack GitHub Presentations & TalksI regularly speak at user groups, webinars, and community events across New Zealand and online. Below is a selection of sessions I have presented. AI & Cloud Sessions Building AI agents and voice-enabled applications with Azure AI services Running LLMs on consumer hardware AI-assisted development and deployment on Azure Application modernisation with Azure and GitHub Copilot Cloud-native pillars: DevOps, containers, serverless, APIs, and data integration Microsoft Events & Webinars From Legacy to Cloud-Native AI-Ready Applications Strategies and tools for transitioning legacy apps, processes, and data to cloud-native and AI-ready technologies. Covers automated code upgrades, re-platforming to Azure, refactoring to cloud-native architectures, DevOps modernisation, zero-trust security, and accelerating modernisation with GitHub Copilot AI agents. AZBC: From Legacy to Cloud-Native AI-Ready Applications From Legacy to Cloud-Native AI-Ready Applications (On-Demand) Recorded Sessions Microsoft Auckland Reactor Pop-Up Developing To Azure Kubernetes Service with Draft Community User Groups & Meetups Auckland .NET User Group Sessions on .NET modernisation, cloud-native patterns, and building with Azure Auckland Azure User Group Deep dives into Azure services, AI architecture, and real-world patterns Software & Developer Community Meetups Talks covering AI agents, containers, Kubernetes, serverless, and developer tooling
